title: Artificial Neuron & Perceptron
subtitle: Contact session 2 · from the biological neuron to the perceptron learning rule, logic gates and the XOR problem

lesson.title: The brain in numbers
lesson.lead: The brain is a mass of interconnected neurons that learn by **association** and compute in **parallel**.

blocks.text: 1 s ÷ 0.001 s = only about **100 sequential steps**, yet we recognise a scene. That's only possible with massive **parallel** computation.
Biological neuron

lesson.title: The artificial neuron
lesson.lead: An artificial neuron computes a **weighted sum plus a bias**, then applies an activation function.

blocks.text: z = Σᵢ wᵢxᵢ + b          ŷ = f(z)

items: Each weight wᵢ shows how important feature xᵢ is.
Knowledge is stored in the **weights** (the connections).
The neuron outputs one number ŷ.

blocks.text: Connectionism

Neural networks are **connectionist machines**: intelligence emerges from many simple units, knowledge is stored in connection weights, and learning changes those weights. Connections can be forward, recursive or self-loops.

lesson.title: When to use a neural network
lesson.lead: ANNs suit high-dimensional, noisy data where the target function is unknown and explainability isn't critical.

items: Input is high-dimensional, discrete or real-valued (raw sensor data).
Data may be noisy or contain errors.
Output is discrete, real-valued or a vector.
The form of the target function is unknown.
Human readability of the result is not important.

blocks.text: Examples: speech recognition, image classification, financial prediction. Properties: many neurons, many weighted connections, highly parallel, weights tuned automatically.

lesson.title: The perceptron
lesson.lead: The perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958) is the simplest neuron: a weighted sum followed by a **step** threshold.

blocks.text: h = w₀ + w₁x₁ + … + wₙxₙ = wᵀx̃        ŷ = 1 if h ≥ 0, else 0
blocks.caption: x̃ = [1, x₁, …, xₙ]: the leading 1 multiplies the bias w₀

blocks.text: Its decision boundary w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ = 0 is a **straight line** (a hyperplane in more dimensions).

blocks.label: Convention
blocks.text: Rosenblatt's original uses outputs **{−1, +1}**; the deck's gate examples use **{0, 1}**. Both work, but the bias/threshold values change. Use whichever the question states.

lesson.title: Logic gates by hand
lesson.lead: Write one inequality per truth-table row, then pick weights that satisfy all of them.

blocks.text: AND
OR
Conditions: w₀ < 0, w₀ + w₂ ≥ 0, w₀ + w₁ ≥ 0, w₀ + w₁ + w₂ ≥ 0. One solution: **w₀ = −1, w₁ = 2, w₂ = 2**.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: Any weights that satisfy every inequality are correct. There are infinitely many separating lines.

lesson.title: The perceptron learning rule
lesson.lead: Only update when the prediction is wrong; move each weight by **η(t − ŷ)xᵢ**.

blocks.text: wᵢ ← wᵢ + η (t − ŷ) xᵢ          b ← b + η (t − ŷ)

items: Initialise the weights (random or zero) and choose η (e.g. 0.1 or 1).
For each example (x, t): compute ŷ.
If ŷ ≠ t, update every weight including the bias.
Repeat epochs until a full pass makes no mistakes (or a max number of epochs).

blocks.label: Key fact
blocks.text: **Convergence theorem:** if the data is linearly separable, the perceptron rule converges in a finite number of steps.
NOT gate, traced (w₀ = w₁ = 0, η = 1)
Final weights: **w₁ = −1, w₀ = 0**.

lesson.title: The XOR problem
lesson.lead: XOR is **not linearly separable**, so no single perceptron can learn it.

blocks.text: The 1s sit on one diagonal and the 0s on the other. No straight line w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0 can put both 1s on one side and both 0s on the other.
Proof sketch: (0,0)→0 needs b < 0; (0,1) and (1,0) need w₂ + b ≥ 0 and w₁ + b ≥ 0; adding these gives w₁ + w₂ + 2b ≥ 0, so w₁ + w₂ + b ≥ −b > 0, which makes (1,1) output 1. Contradiction.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: **Solution:** a multilayer perceptron (hidden layer + non-linear activation). Module 5 builds it.

lesson.title: Linear separability
lesson.lead: Two classes are linearly separable in n-D if an **(n − 1)-dimensional hyperplane** can split them.

items: In 2-D the separator is a line; in 3-D a plane; in n-D a hyperplane.
If one separating line exists, infinitely many do.
AND, OR, NAND, NOR, NOT are separable; XOR (and XNOR) are not.

blocks.label: Homework
blocks.text: Practice from the deck: find perceptron weights for OR, AND, NOR and NAND **using the learning algorithm**. Use the lab bench to check each trace.

worked.title: Verify AND weights

problem.text: Show that w₀ = −1, w₁ = 0.75, w₂ = 0.75 implements AND with ŷ = 1 if h ≥ 0.

worked.answer: All four rows match AND. The decision line is 0.75x₁ + 0.75x₂ = 1.

worked.title: Train OR with the learning rule

problem.text: Train a perceptron for OR from w = (w₀, w₁, w₂) = (0, 0, 0) with η = 1, presenting rows in the order (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).

steps.label: Epoch 3
steps.text: (0,0): h = 0 → 1 ✗ → w = (−1, 1, 1). The other three rows are correct.

worked.answer: w = (w₀, w₁, w₂) = (−1, 1, 1) after 4 epochs. Check it in the Lab bench with gate OR.

problem.text: NOT gate, h = w₀ + w₁x₁, start w₀ = w₁ = 0, η = 1.

steps.label: Epoch 2
steps.text: x = 0: h = −1 → 0 ≠ 1 → w₀ = −1 + 1 = 0 (w₁ unchanged because x = 0). x = 1: h = −1 → 0 ✓.

worked.title: Brain arithmetic

problem.text: Neurons switch in about 0.001 s and scene recognition takes about 1 s. With about 10¹⁰ neurons and 10⁴ connections each, roughly how many connections are there, and what does the timing tell us?

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: 100 steps is far too few for serial processing, so the brain must compute massively in **parallel**.

worked.answer: ≈ 10¹⁴ connections; ≈ 100 serial steps → parallel distributed processing.

labs.title: Perceptron trainer
labs.intro: Pick a gate, set η and the start weights, and run the learning rule epoch by epoch. Watch the decision line move.
tryThis: OR from zeros with η = 1: it should converge to (−1, 1, 1).
AND from zeros with η = 1: count the epochs.
XOR: press "Run until it converges" and see why it never does.
Change η to 0.1: does the number of epochs change for AND?
